name: Acid–Base Balance Calculator (ABG)
seoDesc: An arterial blood gas reports pH, CO₂ and bicarbonate, and the acid–base balance comes from comparing them. Free acid–base balance (abg) calculator: enter you
summary:
An arterial blood gas reports pH, CO₂ and bicarbonate, and the acid–base balance comes from comparing them. It returns anion gap, albumin-corrected gap, expected PaCO₂ (Winter's formula) and base excess estimate, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator gives the anion gap, the respiratory compensation expected for a metabolic acidosis, and flags the classic mixed disorders. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Acid–Base Balance (ABG)
sections.html:
Anion gap = Na⁺ − Cl⁻ − HCO₃⁻; Winter's formula: expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
AGanion gapmmol/L
PaCO₂arterial carbon dioxide tensionmmHg
HCO₃⁻bicarbonatemmol/L
BEbase excessmmol/L

Where the relationship comes from. Winter's formula and the albumin correction for the anion gap are standard bedside acid–base rules.

sections.title: How do I use the Acid–Base Balance (ABG)?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: ph of 7.32, paco₂ of 28 mmHg, bicarbonate of 14 mmol/L, sodium of 140 mmol/L, chloride of 105 mmol/L, albumin of 40 g/L.

Substituting them into the formula gives anion gap of 21 mmol/L, albumin-corrected gap of 111 mmol/L, expected paco₂ (winter's formula) of 29 mmHg, base excess estimate of -10.38 mmol/L, measured minus winter-predicted paco2 of -1 mmHg.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
AG 8 – 12Normalno unmeasured anion accumulation
AG 12 – 20Raisedketoacidosis, lactate, renal failure
AG above 20Higha large unmeasured anion load

  • Winter's formula predicts the CO₂ a metabolic acidosis should produce: a measured CO₂ above the predicted range means a coexisting respiratory acidosis, below it a respiratory alkalosis.

  • The anion gap falls by about 2.5 mmol/L for every 10 g/L of albumin below normal, so a 'normal' gap in a hypoalbuminaemic patient may be a raised gap.

  • Base excess is the metabolically interesting number because it is independent of the respiratory component.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Interpreting pH without checking whether the CO₂ and bicarbonate changes are in the same direction.
  • Ignoring albumin when the anion gap is normal.
  • Using venous values for oxygenation calculations.

sections.html:

Acid-base balance. Osmolarity. Blood pressure.

faq.q: What is a normal anion gap?
faq.a: About 8–12 mmol/L, higher if the laboratory measures chloride by a different method.

faq.q: How do I recognise a mixed disorder?
faq.a: When the measured CO₂ or bicarbonate does not match the compensation the primary disorder should produce.

faq.q: What does the Acid–Base Balance (ABG) actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns anion gap, albumin-corrected gap, expected PaCO₂ (Winter's formula) and base excess estimate. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
